title: China Squeezes India Out of Russian Crude as Iran Imports Collapse; Diesel Cracks Hit Triple Digits
subhead: Beijing is absorbing Russian barrels India used to buy to replace crushed Iranian supply, while US diesel crack spreads hit a record $102 and Brent tops $93 as the Iran-US impasse hardens.

sections.heading: China Diverts Russian Crude Away From India as Iran Barrels Vanish
sections.body:
China is pulling Russian crude out of the market segment India has long relied on, according to Kpler data cited by Reuters. China's seaborne imports of Russian crude are estimated at 1.25 million barrels per day in August, down from 1.423 million bpd in July, but still among its strongest months since April. The shift is geographic: Russian crude loaded from European ports is expected to account for 31% of China's seaborne Russian imports in August, up from 22% in June — directly into the western-port supply lane India traditionally dominates.

India's Russian imports have fallen to an estimated 1.87 million bpd in August, down sharply from a record 2.79 million bpd in July, with imports from European ports down about 770,000 bpd, or nearly 30%. India's total crude imports are pegged at just 4.17 million bpd, the lowest since the Iran war began and down from 5.06 million bpd in July. Chinese imports of Iranian oil, meanwhile, are expected to reach just 340,000 bpd this month, roughly one-third of the 1.14 million bpd imported in March, as the US blockade and Middle East war crush Tehran's flows.
sections.whyItMatters: Two Asian giants are now competing directly for a shrinking pool of Russian crude. India is the more exposed — it lacks China's alternative supply options, and if it cannot replace these barrels by September, its fuel exports could be the next casualty in an Asian product market already short of diesel and gasoline.

sections.heading: Brent Tops $93 as US Tightens the Screws on Iran
sections.body:
Brent crude rose 1.95% to $93.48 a barrel early Thursday, a three-week high, extending a five-day rally, OilPrice reports. WTI traded 2% higher above $85, at $86.12. The move came after President Trump threatened Iran with the 'most crushing economic operation ever taken against any country' and warned that countries helping Iran would face 'TREMENDOUS Economic Consequences.' Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent promised the 'toughest sanctions in history' against Iran, per CNBC, while acknowledging oil markets had misread the pressure campaign.

The real stress is downstream, not in crude. The US diesel crack spread hit triple digits for the first time ever, jumping to as high as $102 a barrel on Monday before easing to about $100. 'Crude is available, diesel is not,' wrote Ole Hansen of Saxo Bank, arguing the market is underestimating the actual supply disruption in fuels even as Brent holds well below the conflict's earlier peaks.
sections.whyItMatters: The crude price tells only part of the story. With refining capacity stretched and Hormuz transit impaired, fuel prices — diesel above all — are where the war's cost is actually landing on consumers and importers, and where Washington's domestic political exposure is greatest.

sections.heading: Washington Eases Gasoline Rules While Sanctioning Tehran
sections.body:
The EPA on Thursday authorized an early switch to cheaper winter-grade gasoline, allowing sales of 10%-ethanol blend starting September 1 rather than mid-September, OilPrice reports. The administration says ending summer-blend requirements early could add hundreds of thousands of barrels per day to domestic gasoline supply. Average US pump prices have held above $4 a gallon since mid-July, roughly $1 higher than when the Iran war began, according to AAA.

The waiver sits awkwardly beside the escalation against Tehran: it came the same day Bessent pledged the harshest sanctions yet, and follows earlier moves to extend a Jones Act shipping waiver through August and broaden E15 gasoline sales. The Energy Department already expects elevated fuel prices to persist through year-end, having revised its outlook higher as Washington and Tehran failed to agree on reopening the Strait of Hormuz.
sections.whyItMatters: The administration is trying to squeeze Tehran without squeezing American motorists — clawing back supply wherever it can find it, one fuel rule at a time, because none of these measures reopen Hormuz. It reveals the domestic political ceiling on the sanctions campaign.

sections.heading: Tajikistan Turns to Iran as Russia's Fuel Crisis Spreads to Central Asia
sections.body:
Tajikistan has requested to import 2.55 million tons of oil and fuels from Iran — including 2 million tons of crude, 150,000 tons of gasoline, 300,000 tons of diesel, and 100,000 tons of jet fuel — according to Tajikistan's Transport Ministry, as the fuel crisis in Russia chokes supply from what was its largest supplier. 'More than 80% of Tajikistan's fuel previously came from Russia,' Transport Minister Azim Ibrohim said. Dushanbe signed more than a dozen cooperation agreements with Tehran this week, hours before Trump's warning about consequences for countries helping Iran.

Russia has banned diesel, gasoline, and jet fuel exports except for inter-governmental supply deals, and has been grappling with shortages for more than three months as Ukrainian drone strikes repeatedly knock out refineries, OilPrice reports. The collapse has left Central Asian states that depended on Russian fuel scrambling for alternatives.
sections.whyItMatters: A Central Asian state is now turning to a sanctioned Iran for fuel because Russia can no longer supply it — a striking reversal that illustrates how Ukraine's refinery-strike campaign is fragmenting Moscow's own energy client base and pushing its neighbors into Iran's orbit, at a moment Washington is trying to isolate Tehran.

sections.heading: Supertanker Prices Hit Records as Gulf Exporters Buy Their Own Fleets
sections.body:
Both new and second-hand very large crude carriers reached prices above $130 million in the second quarter, an all-time high, the Financial Times reports, citing shipbroker Braemar. Annual charter rates for supertankers have also hit records. The surge is driven by Middle East producers moving oil on their own vessels as shipping majors grow wary of transiting Hormuz amid frequent attacks on shipping.

ADNOC earlier this month bought six supertankers and five very large gas carriers for $1.3 billion, and along with Kuwait Petroleum has been using shuttles to move oil to tankers waiting in the Gulf of Oman. ADNOC also issued its ninth spot tender since June this week, offering Upper Zakum, Umm Lulu, and Das crude for October-November loadings; its prior eight tenders sold an estimated more than 100 million barrels. The UAE, which left OPEC on May 1, produced a record 4.1 million bpd in June. By contrast, Iraq — which lacks its own tankers — has had to offer deep discounts to motivate buyers to brave the strait, even as it maintains exports of about 2 million bpd, per its state oil marketing company.
sections.whyItMatters: Ownership of tankers is becoming a geopolitical asset: producers with their own fleets (the UAE, Kuwait) can keep exports flowing through the chokepoint, while those dependent on international shippers (Iraq) must pay a war-risk premium in the form of discounts. This is reshaping who controls the physical oil trade, not just its price.

sections.heading: Coal India Opens a Singapore Front in the Critical Minerals Race
sections.body:
Coal India, the world's largest coal producer, has applied to establish a trading office in Singapore to trade critical minerals and iron ore — its first trading hub outside India — Reuters reports, citing sources. The move is part of a push by Indian state-owned firms to secure strategic mineral assets abroad and cut dependence on Chinese supply.

Indian companies are scouting bauxite and lithium assets in Chile and Australia, with African assets also under review. Earlier this month Reuters reported Coal India was weighing the purchase of a unit of Canada's Wealth Minerals with lithium assets in Chile. New Delhi has moved $10 billion into rare earths this year to reduce China's dominance in the mineral supply chain, and signed a lithium cooperation MoU with Argentina last year.
sections.whyItMatters: The critical minerals scramble is going global and institutional: India's biggest coal miner is now a would-be lithium and minerals trader, positioning New Delhi to compete directly with China for battery metals even as it remains deeply dependent on fossil fuel imports. The energy transition and the old oil economy are converging in India's industrial policy.

sections.heading: Chinese Refiners Snap Up Iraqi Crude as Gulf Routes Fracture
sections.body:
Chinese refiners have bought 8 million barrels of Basrah Heavy and Basrah Medium for prompt delivery, Bloomberg reports, citing traders, as Beijing scrambles for barrels amid fractured Gulf supply routes. Hormuz vessel crossings fell to 95 in the week to August 17, down from 118 the prior week, per Marine Traffic, with some tankers turning off transponders to evade tracking.

Saudi Arabia has diverted exports first from Hormuz to the Red Sea, then from Yanbu to Egypt, and is now shipping crude north through the Suez Canal to avoid Houthi strikes — a route with lower tanker capacity than Bab el-Mandeb. Japanese crude imports also hit an all-time high in July at $76.39 billion, up 27.8% year-on-year, Reuters reports, as elevated oil prices swell import bills across Asia.
sections.whyItMatters: Every Gulf producer is rerouting supply through a different bottleneck — Suez for the Saudis, Hormuz dark-shipments for the UAE, discounted Basrah for Iraq — while Asia absorbs the cost. The war is fragmenting what was once a single Gulf supply system into a patchwork of riskier, costlier routes.

bottomLine: The Iran-US confrontation is now reshaping who gets crude, not just what it costs. China has stepped in to absorb Russian barrels India used to buy, replacing the Iranian supply the blockade has crushed, and India's September fuel exports are the likely next casualty. Meanwhile the real price signal has shifted downstream — US diesel cracks hit a record $102 even as Brent hovers near $93 — and Washington is easing gasoline rules at home while promising its toughest sanctions yet on Tehran. On the fringes, Tajikistan turning to Iran for fuel, tanker owners cashing in at record prices, and Coal India opening a Singapore critical-minerals hub all show the war accelerating the reordering of supply chains across oil, fuel, and transition minerals alike.
sources: OilPrice.com (Julianne Geiger, Charles Kennedy, Tsvetana Paraskova, Irina Slav), Reuters, Kpler, Bloomberg, Financial Times, Braemar, Marine Traffic, CNBC, ING, Saxo Bank (Ole Hansen), AAA, EPA, Tajikistan Transport Ministry, Zawya
